lead: A wing gets shallower from root to tip. Its spar caps are then not parallel to the span, so the axial force in each cap has a component across the beam, and part of the shear force is carried by the caps instead of the web. The web shear flow is no longer S/h. This chapter finds the share the booms take, works it at three stations of a tapered spar, and shows that the web is often most loaded well outboard of the root.
prereq: You need: boom stresses and the shear flow sum of the idealisation chapter.

sections.h3: Boom forces have a component across the beam

blocks.text: Idealise the beam into booms carrying direct stress and panels carrying shear. At a section, boom r carries an axial force P<sub>z,r</sub> = σ<sub>r</sub> B<sub>r</sub> along the beam axis, with σ<sub>r</sub> from the bending formula. If the boom is inclined to the z axis, the actual force runs along the boom, and it has components in the plane of the section:
P<sub>y,r</sub> = P<sub>z,r</sub> (δy<sub>r</sub>/δz),   P<sub>x,r</sub> = P<sub>z,r</sub> (δx<sub>r</sub>/δz),   P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>z,r</sub> √(1 + (δx<sub>r</sub>/δz)² + (δy<sub>r</sub>/δz)²)
blocks.where: P<sub>z,r</sub> is the component of the boom force along z (N), tension positive; δy<sub>r</sub>/δz and δx<sub>r</sub>/δz are the slopes of boom r in the yz and xz planes (dimensionless); P<sub>y,r</sub> and P<sub>x,r</sub> are the components across the section (N); P<sub>r</sub> is the force along the boom.

blocks.text: Taper angles are small, so P<sub>r</sub> ≈ P<sub>z,r</sub>, but the components across the section are not small compared with the shear force. They carry part of S<sub>y</sub> and S<sub>x</sub>, so the webs and skins carry only the rest:
S<sub>y,w</sub> = S<sub>y</sub> − Σ P<sub>y,r</sub>,   S<sub>x,w</sub> = S<sub>x</sub> − Σ P<sub>x,r</sub>
blocks.where: S<sub>y,w</sub> and S<sub>x,w</sub> are the shear forces carried by the walls (N). The wall shear flows then follow from the idealised-section sum with S<sub>y,w</sub> and S<sub>x,w</sub> in place of S<sub>y</sub> and S<sub>x</sub>.

blocks.text: Take a spar of two booms a distance h apart, with the neutral axis midway. Each boom is at y = ±h/2, so I<sub>xx</sub> = 2B(h/2)² and P<sub>z</sub> = M y B/I<sub>xx</sub> = M/h: the boom area cancels. If the depth falls towards the tip at the rate h′ = −dh/dz (positive), each boom slopes towards the centre line at h′/2.

In the usual case, a cantilever whose depth is largest where the moment is largest, the tension boom and the compression boom both lean so that their components across the beam act with the web, against the load. Together they carry M h′/h, so:
S<sub>w</sub> = S − M h′/h,   q = S<sub>w</sub>/h
blocks.where: S is the shear force at the section (N); M the bending moment (N·mm); h the boom spacing (mm); h′ the rate at which the depth falls outboard (dimensionless); q the web shear flow (N/mm).

blocks.text: The same answer comes from boom equilibrium. The web flow equals the rate at which a boom loses force along the span, q = −dP/dz. With P = M/h, dP/dz = (dM/dz)/h − (M/h²)(dh/dz), and dM/dz = −S for z running outboard from the root of a tip-loaded cantilever. The first term alone is the uniform-beam flow S/h; the second is the taper correction.

sections.h3: Wings: taper, sweep and the shear centre

blocks.text: In a wing box with many booms, every boom whose height changes with z takes part of the shear. Compute P<sub>z,r</sub> from the bending stress at the station, multiply by its slope, subtract the sum from S<sub>y</sub>, and use the remainder in the ordinary shear flow calculation. If the booms taper in plan as well, the x slopes take part of S<sub>x</sub> in the same way.

For a linear taper h′ is constant, but the correction M h′/h depends on M/h, which falls towards the tip. So the web flow often rises outboard even as the shear force stays constant: in the example the web flow at the tip is almost three times its root value. Sweep alone, a boom leaning only in plan at constant height, changes none of the P<sub>y</sub> terms; its P<sub>x</sub> components form a couple with the other booms and add a torque. Because the boom share depends on M while the web share depends on S, the line of action of the web resultant shifts with the ratio M/S, so a strongly tapered box has no fixed shear centre.

figure.caption: The worked tapered spar. Left: the booms converge towards the tip, so their 200 kN root forces each lean at 0.02 and together carry 8 kN of the 20 kN shear. Right: the web flow (solid) is 60 N/mm at the root, 93.75 N/mm at mid-span and 166.7 N/mm at the tip, below the untapered S/h (dashed) wherever the moment is not zero.

spec.aria: Left: a side view of a spar whose two booms converge from 200 millimetres apart at the root to 120 at the tip, with a 20 kilonewton downward load at the tip. The top boom carries 200 kilonewtons tension and the bottom 200 kilonewtons compression at the root. A note says each boom slopes 0.02 and at the root they carry 8 kilonewtons of the shear. Right: a graph of web shear flow against distance from the root, rising from 60 newtons per millimetre at the root through 93.75 at mid-span to 166.7 at the tip, with a dashed curve for S over h lying above it and meeting it at the tip.

examples.question: A cantilever spar 2 m long has two booms of 800 mm² each, 200 mm apart at the root and 120 mm at the tip, tapering linearly. A load of 20 kN acts at the tip. Find the boom forces, the share of the shear carried by the booms, and the web shear flow at the root, at mid-span and at the tip.
steps: Depth falls by 80 mm over 2000 mm: h′ = 0.04, so each boom slopes at 0.02. The shear force is 20 kN everywhere; M = 20 kN × (distance from the tip).
Root: M = 40 kN·m, h = 200 mm. P = M/h = 40 × 10⁶/200 = 200,000 N (tension in the top boom, compression in the bottom). Boom stress 250 N/mm².
Each boom carries P × 0.02 = 4,000 N across the beam; together 8,000 N. The web carries S<sub>w</sub> = 20,000 − 8,000 = 12,000 N, and q = 12,000/200 = 60.0 N/mm. A uniform spar would give 100 N/mm.
Mid-span (1 m from the root): h = 160 mm, M = 20 kN·m, P = 125,000 N, booms carry 2 × 2,500 = 5,000 N, web 15,000 N, q = 93.75 N/mm.
Tip: h = 120 mm, M = 0, so the booms carry nothing across the beam and q = 20,000/120 = 166.7 N/mm.
examples.answer: Web flow 60 N/mm at the root (booms take 8 kN), 93.75 N/mm at mid-span and 166.7 N/mm at the tip; root boom force 200 kN.

traps: Using S/h in a tapered web. At the root of the example that gives 100 N/mm against the true 60 N/mm.
Assuming the web is most loaded at the root. Here the tip web flow is 166.7 N/mm.
Writing P = M y/I<sub>xx</sub> without the boom area. That is the stress; the force is σ B.
Taking the slope as 80 instead of 0.04. Both lengths must be in the same unit.
Subtracting the boom share when the beam deepens towards the tip. Then the components add to the web shear; check the direction from a sketch of each boom force.

quiz.q: Write the shear carried by the walls of a tapered beam.
quiz.a: S<sub>y,w</sub> = S<sub>y</sub> − Σ P<sub>z,r</sub> (δy<sub>r</sub>/δz), where P<sub>z,r</sub> is the axial force in boom r and δy<sub>r</sub>/δz its slope.

quiz.q: Why does the boom area cancel in the boom force of a two-boom spar?
quiz.a: I<sub>xx</sub> = 2B(h/2)², so P = M(h/2)B/I<sub>xx</sub> = M/h. The pair of booms carries the moment as a couple, whatever their size.

quiz.q: A two-boom spar is 300 mm deep at a station where the depth falls at 0.04 outboard. M = 60 kN·m and S = 20 kN there. Find the web shear flow.
In the example, what force does the top root boom carry along its own axis?
quiz.a: P<sub>r</sub> = P<sub>z</sub> √(1 + 0.02²) = 200,000 × 1.0002 = 200,040 N, practically the same as P<sub>z</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does the web flow in the example rise from root to tip although the shear force is constant?
quiz.a: The booms carry M h′/h, which is largest at the root where M is large and falls to zero at the tip. The depth also falls, so S<sub>w</sub>/h grows: 60, 93.75 and 166.7 N/mm.

quiz.q: Explain why a strongly tapered box has no single shear centre.
quiz.a: The web resultant carries S − M h′/h and the booms carry M h′/h. The split, and so the line of action of the wall flows, depends on M/S at the station, which changes along the span and between load cases.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real wings taper in depth and in plan at once and are swept, so stress models keep the full three-dimensional direction of each boom. Search for "tapered wing box shear flow".
